nameStory: The 'amber' in this fungus's name comes from its gorgeous honey-colored, translucent appearance that glows like fossilized tree resin when backlit by sunlight. The 'jelly' part is obvious once you touch it - this squishy, gelatinous fungus feels exactly like firm Jell-O and wobbles similarly when poked.
description: American Amber Jelly Fungus is a distinctive gelatinous fungus that looks like golden-brown, translucent blobs attached to dead branches and twigs. These rubbery, jelly-like growths are typically top-shaped or turbinate, meaning they're wider at the top and narrower where they attach to wood. They're small fungi, usually just an inch or two across, but their unique texture and amber coloration make them unmistakable. Unlike typical mushrooms with caps and stems, these are simply wobbly masses of jelly-like fungal tissue.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels exactly like firm gelatin or rubber - squishy, bouncy, and translucent when fresh, becoming harder and darker when dried out

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Honey-amber to orange-brown, often with a beautiful translucent quality that glows when light passes through it

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Top-shaped or turbinate - broader at the top, narrowing to a point where it attaches to the wood substrate

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found growing on dead, still-attached twigs and branches of broadleaved trees like oak, maple, and birch

idTips.label: Surface
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface when moist, may develop wrinkled or folded areas, no gills, pores, or other structures

idTips.label: Safety
idTips.description: Never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification - while not known to be toxic, jelly fungi are not commonly consumed

habitat: Look for American Amber Jelly Fungus on dead but still-attached branches of hardwood trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It's particularly common on oak, maple, birch, and beech branches, usually growing 3-15 feet off the ground on twigs and smaller branches rather than main trunks. You'll find it in both mature forests and forest edges, from sea level to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Begins appearing as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. Fresh specimens are plump, translucent, and beautifully amber-colored.
seasonality.summer: Continues fruiting after summer rains, though hot, dry periods may cause existing specimens to shrink and darken temporarily until rewetted.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding fresh specimens as autumn moisture returns. Look for them on freshly fallen branches after storms.
seasonality.winter: Persists through mild winter weather, becoming darker and more rubbery in cold, but reviving with moisture during thaws.

funFact: This remarkable fungus can essentially come back from the dead - when dried specimens look completely shriveled and black, just add water and watch them plump back up to their original amber jelly-like state within hours, as if nothing happened!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other jelly fungi like Black Witches' Butter, but American Amber Jelly stays consistently amber to orange-brown rather than turning black. Remember: amber equals American Amber Jelly, black equals Black Witches' Butter.
contextualKnowledge: The common name 'amber jelly roll' used in some references might make you expect a rolled or cylindrical shape, but don't be misled - this fungus is actually top-shaped rather than rolled, and the 'roll' likely just refers to its general jelly-like wobbliness.
compareHints: American Amber Jelly differs from its close relative Black Witches' Butter by staying consistently amber to orange-brown rather than turning black with age. While Birch Jelly tends to be more button-shaped and yellowish, American Amber Jelly is distinctly top-shaped and maintains its rich amber coloration. The turbinate shape and consistent amber color are the best ways to distinguish it from other Exidia species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black Witches' Butter stands out from its Exidia relatives by its distinctly warty, blister-like surface texture and preference for oak wood.

Amber jelly differs from its relatives mainly by substrate preference - while Black Witches' Butter grows on various hardwoods and appears darker, and birch jelly sticks to birch trees, amber jelly is the willow specialist.
